Lesson ☆

VFR airspace at a glance

What you need to enter each class of airspace, what your airplane needs to carry, and the weather you need to see. One table to keep on your kneeboard, with the Bay Area examples you will fly through on your first cross-country.

On this page

The one-page version Three things students get wrong Where to look on the chart Before your next flight

The one-page version

Class Bay Area examples To enter Equipment VFR visibility and cloud clearance
A 18,000 ft MSL up to FL600, everywhere IFR clearance; instrument rating Transponder with Mode C and ADS-B Out Not applicable — VFR is not permitted
B San Francisco (SFO) An explicit ATC clearance into Class B; student pilots need an endorsement first Two-way radio; Mode C transponder and ADS-B Out (also within the 30 nm Mode C veil) 3 SM; clear of clouds
C San Jose (SJC), Oakland (OAK) Two-way radio communication established with ATC before entry Two-way radio; Mode C transponder and ADS-B Out 3 SM; 500 ft below, 1,000 ft above, 2,000 ft horizontal
D Palo Alto (PAO), San Carlos (SQL), Hayward (HWD), Livermore (LVK), Reid-Hillview (RHV), Moffett (NUQ) Two-way radio communication established with the tower before entry Two-way radio 3 SM; 500 below, 1,000 above, 2,000 horizontal
E below 10,000 ft MSL Most of the airspace between the Class D rings and the mountains Nothing for VFR ADS-B Out above 10,000 ft MSL (except within 2,500 ft of the surface) 3 SM; 500 below, 1,000 above, 2,000 horizontal
E at or above 10,000 ft MSL Crossing the Sierra Nothing for VFR ADS-B Out 5 SM; 1,000 below, 1,000 above, 1 SM horizontal
G at or below 1,200 ft AGL Under the Class E floor away from airports Nothing Nothing Day: 1 SM, clear of clouds. Night: 3 SM; 500 / 1,000 / 2,000
G above 1,200 ft AGL, below 10,000 ft MSL Rare around the Bay; common in the Central Valley and foothills Nothing Nothing Day: 1 SM; 500 / 1,000 / 2,000. Night: 3 SM; 500 / 1,000 / 2,000
G above 1,200 ft AGL and at or above 10,000 ft MSL High terrain in the Sierra Nothing Nothing 5 SM; 1,000 below, 1,000 above, 1 SM horizontal

Sources: §91.155 basic VFR weather minimums, §91.215 transponder, §91.225 ADS-B Out, §91.129–91.131 Class D, C and B operations, AIM Chapter 3.

Three things students get wrong

"Radio contact" is not "radio communication established." For Class C and D you need the controller to say your call sign back to you. "Aircraft calling, stand by" with your call sign counts; "aircraft calling, stand by" without it does not. If they have not said your call sign, stay outside.

Class B is different. A Class B entry requires the words "cleared into the Class Bravo." Being in contact, being told to stand by, even being given a squawk code — none of that is a clearance. As a student pilot you also need a specific endorsement for the Class B you are entering, and you may not take off or land at SFO at all (§91.131 and Part 91 Appendix D).

The Mode C veil is bigger than the Class B. Within 30 nautical miles of SFO you need Mode C and ADS-B Out even when you are well below and outside the Class B shelves — which means nearly every Bay Area training flight.

Where to look on the chart

  • The Class B is the solid blue lines with the floor and ceiling written as hundreds of feet, for example 100/30 means 10,000 ft down to 3,000 ft.
  • Class C is solid magenta with the same kind of numbers.
  • Class D is a dashed blue ring; the ceiling is in a bracket, for example [25].
  • Class E starting at the surface is a dashed magenta ring. Class E starting at 700 ft AGL is the shaded magenta fade; where there is no shading at all, Class E starts at 1,200 ft AGL.
  • Everything else, below those floors, is Class G.

Print the Aeronautical Chart Users' Guide legend and keep it in your flight bag until you no longer need it.

Before your next flight

Open the San Francisco sectional. Trace the flight from TBDbase airport to a non-towered airport you would like to visit and write down, leg by leg, which class of airspace you are in, what you need to say, and the lowest weather you would accept. Bring it to our next lesson and we will fly it.
